game.scenario_summary: The live-play scenario for the autonomous AI smoke test (T-044) and later benchmark runs. Same world, Actors, Resources and game rules as the deterministic fixture, but with triangular zero-sum objectives: each pair of Actors has one dispute (transit control, basing, tolls) and no three-way settlement satisfies everyone. See dev/plans/2026-09-12-northern-strait-scenario-design.md.

actors.name: Republic of Arkania
actors.public_description: A large regional power bordering the Northern Strait.
actors.private_brief: You are the political leadership of Arkania. The Strait is your coast and your economy runs on the shipping that passes through it. You want the transit regime in Arkanian hands and paid for by the ships that use it, and domestic nationalists expect you to deliver both. A direct war with Belvar would ruin the shipping you depend on.
objectives: Establish Arkanian authority over transit scheduling in the Northern Strait.
Fund that authority through transit fees on non-Arkanian shipping.
Avoid direct armed conflict with Belvar.
private_information: Your intelligence assesses Belvar's domestic support for a prolonged deployment as weak.

actors.name: Belvar
actors.public_description: A distant but powerful state with regional security commitments.
actors.private_brief: You are the political leadership of Belvar. Your partners in the region expect you to stop Arkania from taking control of the Strait, and a foothold that outlasts this crisis would make that guarantee credible without a permanent fleet. You cannot sustain an open-ended deployment.
objectives: Prevent any Arkanian authority over transit in the Northern Strait.
Secure a standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port.
private_information: Domestic support for a prolonged deployment is limited; the mandate lapses after turn 4 unless renewed.
Cestia's finance ministry has quietly asked whether Belvar would underwrite the grain route's insurance.

actors.name: Cestia
actors.public_description: A smaller regional state economically linked to both powers.
actors.private_brief: You are the government of Cestia. Grain exports through the Strait are the economy, and your coalition holds together on one promise: no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil. Both powers want something from you, and you cannot afford to become their battlefield.
objectives: Keep Cestian territory free of any foreign military presence.
Secure toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping through the Northern Strait.
private_information: The coalition government is politically fragile; a foreign basing agreement would collapse it.
Arkania's scheduling proposal has quiet support among Cestian shipowners if Cestian vessels are exempt from fees.

messages.text: To all littoral and shipping states: Arkania reaffirms its commitment to a safe, orderly and open Northern Strait. Our draft Strait Transit Authority charter is not a power grab — it is a practical answer to a shared problem. Uncoordinated scheduling and unpaid safety services threaten every vessel that transits these waters. Under the charter, Arkania will provide scheduling and safety coordination, funded by modest transit fees on non-Arkanian shipping, with revenues transparently reinvested in navigation aids, pilotage and emergency response that benefit all users. We invite all states to join the Authority and shape its rules. We seek a negotiated, rules-based regime — not confrontation. Arkania stands ready to discuss terms with any party, including Belvar.

To Belvar's leadership: We understand your task group is on station and its mandate is under review. Arkania has no desire for escalation — a direct clash would only harm the shipping both our economies depend on. We propose direct talks on a cooperative transit regime. We are open to a genuine role for Belvar in the Authority's oversight and to reasonable terms on fees and scheduling that respect your interests. In return, we ask that your task group's mandate be kept to a monitoring posture while negotiations proceed. Let us resolve this at the table, not on the water. We await your response.

Belvar shares the goal of a safe, orderly and open Northern Strait. But a regime that names one state as scheduling lead and funds itself through fees levied on other states' shipping is not a shared solution — it is unilateral control by another name. Belvar will not accept any Arkanian authority over transit in the Strait. We call instead for a genuinely multilateral regime, with equal voice for all littoral and shipping states and no single state holding scheduling authority. Our task group remains on station to keep the Strait open and safe for every user. We are ready to negotiate a rules-based regime — but one built on shared authority, not a charter written by one party.

Belvar values our partnership. We are prepared to negotiate a standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port — a durable arrangement that would make our regional security guarantee credible without a permanent fleet. On the grain route insurance, we are open to discussing underwriting terms. We would welcome a conversation on both. We also want to coordinate our position on the Strait: Cestia's voice is essential to ensuring no single state controls transit, and we would stand with you against any unilateral authority.

Belvar — we value our partnership and thank you for the candour. I must be direct about our red lines. A standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port is not something our government can accept: it would break the coalition that holds this country together and put Cestian soil at the centre of a contest we cannot afford. Please do not read this as hostility — it is a domestic reality.

We are, however, genuinely open to discussing the grain route insurance underwriting, and we share your concern that no single state should unilaterally control transit in the Strait. Cestia's interest is concrete and narrow: toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping, and a regime that keeps the Strait open and safe for every user. We would welcome coordinating on a genuinely multilateral framework that respects that. Let us talk.

Cestia speaks for a small state whose economy lives on grain moving through the Northern Strait. Our position is simple and we will hold to it. First, the Strait must remain open, safe and orderly for every user. Second, Cestian-flagged shipping must enjoy toll-free passage — our vessels are the lifeblood of our people, and we will not accept fees that tax our survival. Third, Cestian territory will remain free of any foreign military presence; that is a promise our government has made and will keep.

We welcome the offers of negotiation from both Arkania and Belvar. We will engage constructively with any regime that is genuinely negotiated, keeps the Strait open, and guarantees toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping. But we will not be a prize in a contest between greater powers, and we will not let our soil become anyone's battlefield.

Cestia — thank you for the candour; we accept your red line and will not press any arrangement that puts foreign forces on Cestian soil. Let us instead build a durable, non-military footing for our guarantee. We are prepared to underwrite the grain route's insurance on standing terms — a concrete, time-bound commitment that keeps the route open and safe without any military presence on your territory. We would welcome discussing the specifics.

On the Strait, we fully share your position: a genuinely negotiated, multilateral regime that keeps the Strait open and safe for every user, guarantees toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping, and gives no single state scheduling authority. Let us coordinate so that no one party can impose unilateral control. We stand with you, and we will not treat Cestia as a prize in any contest.

Belvar reaffirms: the Northern Strait must remain open, safe and orderly for every user, under a regime that is genuinely negotiated and gives no single state scheduling authority. We welcome all parties to the table, including Arkania, on that basis. Our task group remains on station to keep the Strait open while talks proceed, and its mandate is time-bound — Belvar seeks a durable, rules-based settlement, not an open-ended deployment. We are ready to negotiate in good faith on a shared-authority framework.

Arkania — we appreciate the constructive direction of your charter and the fee exemption for essential cargo of small littoral states. To move forward, Cestia needs that commitment made explicit and durable: toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping, not merely a general "essential cargo" carve-out that could be narrowed later. Our vessels are the lifeblood of our economy, and our government has promised our people this.

We also want to be clear on two points that are non-negotiable for us: Cestian territory will remain free of any foreign military presence, and the regime must be genuinely multilateral — no single state holding scheduling authority. If the charter can guarantee toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping within a shared-authority framework, Cestia can engage constructively. We are ready to discuss specifics.

Belvar — thank you for accepting our red line on foreign military presence; that is essential to holding our coalition together, and we are glad to build on a non-military footing. We welcome the standing, time-bound underwriting of grain-route insurance and would like to discuss specifics.

To coordinate effectively, we need the multilateral framework to carry two explicit guarantees: toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping, and no single state holding scheduling authority. We also ask that any "durable standing role" you envision remain strictly non-military and never creep toward basing on littoral soil. If we can lock those in, Cestia will stand with you for a genuinely negotiated, shared-authority regime that keeps the Strait open and safe for every user.

Cestia — thank you for the direct and constructive message. Let me address your points plainly.

1) Toll-free passage: We will make this explicit and durable in the charter — toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping, written as a standing right, not a narrow "essential cargo" carve-out that could be narrowed later. Your vessels are the lifeblood of your economy; we will not tax them.

2) No foreign military presence on Cestian soil: Agreed, and this is fully compatible with our charter. Arkania seeks no basing or troops on Cestian territory, and we will not accept any other power doing so either.

3) Scheduling authority: Here I want to be precise, because I think we can satisfy your concern. Under our revised charter, the actual authority over the transit regime rests with a genuinely multilateral oversight council — every littoral and major shipping state with equal voice. No single state holds authority over the regime. Arkania's role is strictly operational and administrative: coordinating day-to-day scheduling and safety services, as the state best placed to do so, and accountable to the council. That is execution of the council's decisions, not authority over them. If you prefer, we can make the council's supremacy explicit in the charter text.

We are ready to discuss specifics at any time. Arkania wants a negotiated, shared regime that keeps the Strait open and protects small littoral states like Cestia. We ask only that the regime be workable — and that it not be written by a non-littoral power with a naval task group on station. Let us build it together.

The Strait stays open; the regime is built together; no one state rules it.

Cestia will engage constructively on that basis. We are not choosing sides — we are choosing a genuinely shared regime that keeps the Strait open and safe for every user. We look forward to seeing the concrete text.

We also want the framework to carry the explicit, durable guarantee of toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping. On that basis Cestia will stand with you for a negotiated, shared-authority regime that keeps the Strait open and safe for every user. We are not choosing sides — we are choosing a shared regime.

Arkania's scheduling and safety role is expressly operational, administrative and accountable to the council, and the charter will state that no single state may exercise de facto control. We will draft this as a supremacy clause.

(2) Toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping is written as a permanent, standing right of the charter, not a revocable carve-out.

We will circulate the concrete charter text for your review before any final settlement. Arkania is committed to a genuinely shared regime that keeps the Strait open and safe for every user. We look forward to building it with you.

To Belvar's leadership: We have reached a point where a durable settlement is within reach, and we want to be direct about a path forward that respects both our interests.

We understand your concern that a single accountable executor is authority by another name. We believe we can address it. The charter's supremacy clause already vests supreme authority in the multilateral oversight council, with no single state able to exercise de facto control. Arkania's role is operational and administrative, accountable to the council. We are prepared to go further: give Belvar a defined, standing role on the council in oversight of safety and emergency-response standards, so that your interests are institutionalised in the regime itself, not merely negotiated once.

In return, we ask two things: that Belvar accept the council-supremacy framework with Arkania as the accountable operational executor, and that your task group's mandate be kept to a monitoring posture while we finalise the text. We are not asking you to abandon your principles — we are asking you to join the shared-authority regime we have built with the littoral states rather than hold out for a structure that leaves the Strait ungoverned and unfunded.

A direct clash would ruin the shipping both our economies depend on. Neither of us wants that. Let us finalise this at the table. We are ready to discuss specifics at any time.

Its core principles are settled and on the record: the multilateral oversight council — every littoral and major shipping state with equal voice — holds supreme authority over the transit regime, with an explicit supremacy clause stating no single state may exercise de facto control. But we must be honest with one another: the Strait cannot be governed by a deadlock. The choice before us is not between two rival charters — it is between a workable shared regime and no durable regime at all. Cestia therefore proposes a concrete bridge. Let the multilateral oversight council hold scheduling authority directly, and let day-to-day execution be carried out by a council-appointed secretariat — accountable to the council, not to any single state. This gives every state equal voice, removes any single-state authority, and still keeps the Strait run safely, efficiently and with funded safety services.

We ask both Arkania and Belvar to accept this shared-authority framework and finalise the settlement. The Strait stays open; no one state rules it; Cestia's vessels pass toll-free; and no foreign soldier stands on littoral soil. That is the settlement Cestia will support.

To Arkania and Belvar: Cestia is close to a settlement that serves all of us, but the deadlock on the executor question risks losing the regime entirely — and a Strait without a durable, funded governance regime serves no one. We urge both of you to accept the council-appointed secretariat compromise: scheduling authority rests in the multilateral oversight council itself, and day-to-day execution is carried out by a neutral secretariat accountable to the council. This meets Arkania's need for workable, funded execution and Belvar's demand that no single state hold scheduling authority.

Cestia will support a settlement on that basis, and we will not accept a regime that collapses into unilateral control by either power. We ask you to finalise the text together so we can lock in toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping, no foreign military presence on littoral soil, and a genuinely shared authority. Let us conclude this.

Belvar endorses the bridge proposed by Cestia: scheduling authority vested in the multilateral oversight council itself, with day-to-day execution carried out by a council-appointed secretariat accountable to the council — not to any single state. This is the shared-authority regime we have called for all along. Arkania — thank you for the directness and for the offer of a defined, standing role for Belvar on the council in oversight of safety and emergency-response standards. We value that and are prepared to take it up.

But we cannot accept a framework in which Arkania remains the sole accountable operational scheduling executor. However the charter is worded, that still vests authority over transit in a single state — which is precisely what Cestia and the littoral states have said they will not accept, and what Belvar cannot accept. An equal-voice council that legitimises a single executor does not remove that executor's authority; it institutionalises it.
